**Overview**
Proposition 43 would require two-thirds voter approval, instead of a simple majority, for certain special taxes at the local level that voters themselves put forward, starting in 2027. A yes vote approves that change, and a no vote keeps the current majority threshold. Lawmakers placed this constitutional amendment before voters in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election.

**Official title**
"LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT."

**Official summary** (split into two quotes to stay under 125 characters each)
- "Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed"
- "to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027."

**Fiscal impact, as stated** (also split)
- "Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold"
- "for certain taxes."

The page labels this "Fiscal Impact" in its summary but doesn't attribute it to the Legislative Analyst's Office. The full analysis is on a separate "Analysis" page, which isn't included in the content provided.

**Arguments in favor**
Supporters argue the measure would restore the "two-thirds vote requirement" Proposition 13 set for special taxes raised locally, including sales, real estate and utility levies. They say courts have let "special interests" push through earmarked tax hikes with a lower vote threshold. They argue the change closes that gap, shielding taxpayers, owners and tenants, and they urge a yes vote.

**Arguments against**
Opponents argue the measure would weaken voters' capacity to fund core local services such as fire services, 911 dispatch, education, road upkeep, hospitals and "affordable housing." They say it would not lower anyone's taxes and claim it "lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want," which they frame as a threat to majority rule. They urge a no vote.

**Proposition 43 (November 2026 ballot)**
*Source: LAist, by Erin Rode and CalMatters. Updated Nov. 2, 2026.*

**What the measure does**
- Would require two-thirds voter approval, not a bare majority, for local special taxes that citizens propose. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
- Local governments already need two-thirds support for special taxes they propose. This would apply the same standard to citizen initiatives.
- Special taxes fund a designated purpose, such as housing or transit. General taxes support a city's overall budget and can be used more broadly. General taxes need only a majority, whoever proposes them.
- Official title: "Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services." It is a legislative constitutional amendment.
- A yes vote would require two-thirds approval for certain local taxes. A no vote would keep majority approval for them.

**Background**
- The measure stemmed from a pact between state lawmakers and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA), an anti-tax group. The pact aimed to block a stricter tax-limiting plan from the ballot. The article doesn't identify that plan.
- Previously, citizen-led special taxes were presumed to need two-thirds. Since 2017, they have needed only a bit over half.
- The article doesn't explain what drove the 2017 change and doesn't mention any court cases.
- Since then, localities have approved more than two dozen such measures despite falling short of two-thirds, per earlier CalMatters reporting.

**Fiscal effects and local examples**
- Los Angeles: Measure ULA (the "mansion tax") drew 57.77% approval in 2022. Under a two-thirds rule, that result would have fallen short of the roughly 66.7% needed (my calculation).
- LAist also has a guide on Los Angeles Proposition TE, which deals with the mansion tax and fire victims.

- Supporters, including HJTA, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board, argue that special-interest groups have exploited the lower majority bar to pass taxes in elections with few voters.

- Requires two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes, including those placed on the ballot by citizen signature drives, which currently need only a majority.

- Restores the pre-2017 rule that applied to all local special taxes.
- Would not affect measures already on this year's ballot, only future ones.
- Ballot language: "Prop 43 limits voters' ability to raise revenues for local government services."

**Background**
- Prop 13 (late 1970s) required two-thirds approval for special taxes that local governments put to voters.
- Around 2017, a court decision read Prop 13's "government" language as excluding citizen petitions, so those taxes needed only a majority. The article does not name the case or mention Upland.
- The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA), named after the Prop 13 backer, has pushed since then to reverse this, arguing that courts created a loophole that undercut Prop 13's purpose.

**The Howard Jarvis deal**
- Earlier this year, HJTA teamed with developers and real-estate groups to qualify an initiative that would have (1) changed the two-thirds rules for local taxes, (2) limited transfer taxes on property sales, and (3) retroactively wiped out many of them.
- Cities rely on transfer-tax revenue, so local governments opposed the initiative and pushed to negotiate it off the ballot.
- East Bay Democrat Buffy Wicks, an Assembly member, wrote ACA 22, the bill that became Prop 43. It passed the Legislature.
- Wicks opposes the measure herself. She said the vote removes "the greatest threat to our cities and their fiscal health," which she named the Taxpayer Protection Act.
- No legislative vote counts are reported.

**Main arguments**
*For*
- HJTA president Jon Coupal: "whenever the courts create a loophole, we have to come back and shut the door."
- Supporters, including the California Republican Party and other anti-tax groups, say taxes aimed at a specific cause should need broad, two-thirds backing.
- Developers and real-estate groups (backers of the earlier initiative) say transfer taxes have grown excessive and harm development.

*Against*
- California Democratic Party.
- California State Association of Counties and SEIU California, which represents many local government workers who could lose if local revenue becomes harder to raise.
- Core argument: this is a poor time to restrict local revenue, since many cities and counties already face budget strain, and the measure would make it harder for citizens to bring tax measures to voters.

- The article includes no official fiscal estimate or revenue projection for Prop 43.
- Supporters have spent more than $14 million. Much of that came before the measure reached its final form, when it still included the transfer-tax provisions.
- The California Business Roundtable spent over $9 million supporting the effort earlier in 2026, but has not spent since the final version reached the ballot.
- Opposition spending is lower, though no total is given.
- No dollar figures are given for transfer-tax revenue or for the revenue Prop C raised.

**Measures that would have failed under two-thirds**
- The article offers one example: San Francisco's 2018 Prop C, a business tax for homelessness services, won slightly above 60%, short of two-thirds.
- This year's region-wide transit sales-tax measure (for BART, Muni, and Caltrain) needs only a majority, and Prop 43 would not affect it. The article does not say whether it would clear two-thirds.

**Prop. 43 summary**
*Business Journal explainer by Gordon M. Webster Jr., Oct. 27, 2026*

**What it does**
- From Jan. 1, 2027, voter-initiated local special taxes that are new, higher, or extended would need a two-thirds yes vote, the same threshold local agencies already face.
- It leaves existing taxes in place, keeps the general-tax vote rule unchanged, and sets no limit on real estate transfer taxes.
- The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association's first version included a transfer-tax limit, but a June agreement with the governor's team and legislative leaders dropped it. The narrower ACA 22 compromise reached the ballot after 35-1 Senate and 68-2 Assembly votes.

**Background**

**Source:** California Budget & Policy Center, "Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?" (August 2026)

**Stated position**
The Center takes no formal yes or no position. It says it "does not endorse or oppose ballot measures," but adds that the analysis "reflects the institutional position of the Budget Center." The analysis itself is clearly critical. Its key takeaway says the measure would raise the bar for local revenue and "give outsized power to a small share of voters," and it warns that some communities could be left worse off.

**What the measure does**
Special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, whether new, renewed, or increased, would need two-thirds voter approval. The rule would cover a wide range of local and regional bodies, from cities to special districts, for measures placed on local ballots starting January 1, 2027.

**Main reasons**
- **Harder to pass:** Voter-initiated special taxes currently need only a simple majority. The Center says the measure would make passage less likely "even if a significant majority of local voters support the measure."
- **Cuts vs. revenue:** Local governments can cut services without a public vote, but raising revenue requires one. Cities and counties could still pass general taxes with a simple majority, while special districts would face the higher threshold whether or not funds are tied to specific programs.
- **Rising need:** The Center says "H.R. 1 will deeply harm Californians," referring to the 2025 federal law that cuts Medi-Cal and CalFresh funding. It expects counties to be hit hardest, with higher costs and more uninsured patients at county hospitals. It also expects health care districts and public hospitals to be strained, and cities may face greater need for homelessness and affordable housing support. Other pressures include inflation, an aging population, and more frequent climate disasters.

**Examples cited**
The page gives four examples of special-tax initiatives that passed with a simple majority:

| Measure | Year | Purpose | Vote share |
|---|---|---|---|
| San Francisco Measure C | 2018 | Levy on commercial landlords for early childhood programs | 51% |
| Fresno Measure P | 2018 | Sales tax increase for parks | 52% |
| Los Angeles Measure ULA | 2022 | Transfer tax on high-end property sales for housing and homelessness | 58% |
| Madera County Measure T | 2024 | Renewed sales tax for transportation | 52% |

The page doesn't say these would have failed under two-thirds. However, each fell short of the roughly 67% that two-thirds requires, so by simple arithmetic all four would have fallen short had Prop. 43's standard applied. Because the measure covers only ballots from 2027 onward, these are illustrations rather than cases it would govern.

**Fiscal effect**
The Center gives no dollar estimate and doesn't quantify lost revenue or how many measures would be blocked. Its fiscal discussion is qualitative: Prop. 43 would make special-tax revenue harder to raise, while H.R. 1 and other pressures push up costs and demand.

**Majority rule**
The Center argues that supermajority rules let a small minority block measures most voters want. As it puts it, "Supermajority vote requirements allow a small share of voters to block policies favored by a large majority of voters." Its example: "Prop. 43 would allow 35% of local voters to block an initiative that 65% of voters support."

It also notes that statewide measures need only a simple majority, even when they alter the constitution. That lets a narrow statewide majority impose a higher bar on local voters, even though "different communities in the state have different needs and preferences."

**The "Upland issue"**
The page never mentions Upland, so I can't report the Center's view on it. The closest topic is court rulings. The Center says recent decisions made clear that the two-thirds requirement "does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative." That is why voter-initiated special taxes currently pass by simple majority. The Supreme Court declined to review those appellate decisions, leaving them in place.

**Source:** CalMatters, by Yue Stella Yu (October 2026)

**Overview**
Prop. 43 would require "two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes." Supporters see that higher bar as the point. Opponents warn it would choke off money for essential services.

**Background**
- Voters set a two-thirds bar for special taxes in 1996. A 2017 state Supreme Court ruling said it reaches only measures that local officials put on the ballot. The court didn't settle whether citizen-proposed taxes are covered, and several citizen-placed measures have since passed by simple majority.
- Prop. 43 traces back to a clash over Los Angeles's "mansion tax": 4% on real estate sales above $5.3 million and 5.5% above $10.6 million, with rates rising alongside inflation.
- Coupal's group earlier this year pursued a broader measure that would have cut statewide sales taxes on real estate, required two-thirds approval for every special tax, and repealed simple-majority taxes like the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is the scaled-back version negotiated with Democratic legislative leaders. It changes only the vote threshold and isn't retroactive. Separately, the state's high court unanimously blocked a broader 2024 measure from the same group before that election, calling it an unlawful bid to amend the constitution.
- **Upland:** The article never mentions Upland, so there's no Upland background to report. The closest background it gives is the Los Angeles "mansion tax" fight above.

**Supporters**
- **Jon Coupal**, who heads the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA), says Prop. 43 would make explicit that the two-thirds rule covers every special tax. He traces the requirement to the 1849 Constitution, which required a supermajority of lawmakers before asking voters to borrow.
  - "The power to tax is (the) government's most draconian power."
  - "when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus."
  - "We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed."
  - "California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more."
- **HJTA's broader argument:** Anti-tax advocates say "it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians," noting rates already run high. They argue one standard should cover government and citizen-sponsored taxes alike.

**Opponents**
- **Local governments, labor groups and advocates for affordable housing** say the measure would make it hard to fund firefighting, schools and health care. They argue it could enable "minority rule," since a third of voters could block a tax.
- **Darrell Roberts**, who heads the California Professional Firefighters (38,000 members), calls Prop. 43 an "insurmountable roadblock" to funding community services. In a Marin Independent Journal op-ed, he wrote: "Under Prop. 43, it's clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else." He also pointed to a Los Angeles half-cent sales tax for hiring firefighters, on the ballot this November.
- **Buffy Wicks**, the Oakland Democrat who drafted the compromise, now says she is "adamantly opposed." She framed the choice as a retroactive measure that "threatened billions in local funding" versus a narrower amendment she "still believed was bad policy."

**Fiscal picture and examples**
- The article gives no official fiscal estimate of Prop. 43's revenue impact.
- Two examples would not have cleared the threshold: Los Angeles's 2022 "mansion tax" (58% yes) and Sonoma County's 2024 half-cent sales tax for wildfire response and emergency services (62% yes). The article says: "Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43."
- The city says the mansion tax has raised $1.4 billion since 2023.
- Wicks's "billions" refers to the retroactive measure she contrasted with Prop. 43, not to Prop. 43 itself.

**Polling**
- A September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) found 51% of likely voters opposed Prop. 43 and 43% in favor.
- Coupal is counting on voters' affordability frustrations to help the measure.

**Spending**
- Supporters: almost $15 million. The California Business Roundtable PAC contributed close to $10 million of that.
- Opponents: $6 million, including a $1.5 million top gift from a PAC linked to SEIU California.

Your numbers check out, but the scope needs a caveat.

- PPIC's October 2026 statewide survey found 42% of likely voters in favor of Prop 43 and 55% opposed.
- Against September's split, the yes share dipped a point and the no share climbed four.
- Party and age divide the electorate sharply: 68% of Republicans, 41% of independents, and 28% of Democrats back it, while backing reaches 30% among 18–34-year-olds and 50% among those 55 and older. No region reaches a majority.
- Sources describe the scope differently: PPIC frames the change as reaching local special taxes generally, whereas Berkeley IGS's guide ties the two-thirds threshold (66.67%) to citizen-initiated measures, and a Business Journal explainer dates it to 2027.
- Backers present it as a fix for legal workarounds that had let citizen-led levies pass by majority alone.
- Opponents warn it could leave fire departments short-staffed and slow emergency response.
- The No campaign's release repeats those figures, so PPIC's page is the better primary source.

Voters decide Prop 43 today (Nov. 3, 2026), so these are pre-election numbers. The results didn't include October's sample size or margin of error, or the Berkeley IGS poll's figures.

**Vote threshold: majority.** The court did not hold that Measure ULA needed two-thirds approval. It "passed with 57.77% of the vote," and the court held that passage by majority vote was valid. This holding is in the published portion.

**Disposition:** "The order of dismissal is affirmed," and respondents get their appeal costs. Benabou's other challenges also failed, in the unpublished portion.

**Key holding language (excerpted):**
- Vote: "passage of Measure ULA pursuant to a majority vote of the City's electorate was a valid exercise"
- Section 4: it restricts local governments, but "it does not limit the ability of voters to do so via initiative."
- Transaction taxes: section 4 "did not impliedly revoke the local initiative power with respect to special real property transaction taxes."
- Charter section 450(a): it "does not clearly and unambiguously revoke the people's initiative power."

**Reasoning:**
- **Section 4 reaches only local governments.** Earlier decisions found its two-thirds rule inapplicable to initiatives, and the court extended that logic to the transaction-tax ban.
- **Charter section 450(a) doesn't limit initiatives.** At oral argument, Howard Jarvis dropped the claim that section 4 itself reaches initiatives. It then argued that section 450(a) did so implicitly. The court disagreed: that section never mentions transaction taxes or section 4, and its history shows no such intent.
- **Clear-statement rule.** Drawing on *Upland* and *Kennedy Wholesale*, courts presume against limits on initiative power and won't infer one without a "clear, unambiguous indication." Because section 4 came from Proposition 13, the court applied *Kennedy Wholesale*'s reasoning: that history doesn't show voters meant to restrict their own taxing power.
- **Exception acknowledged.** Local initiative power generally tracks the legislative body's power, but the court called this case an exception. Local governments are barred from these taxes, while voters aren't.

**Article XIII C, section 2:** The opinion doesn't analyze this provision for Measure ULA. It appears only in describing *Upland*, where the Supreme Court found it didn't restrict voters' taxing power through statutory initiatives. ULA's validity rests on section 4 and charter section 450(a).

**Special or general:** The court treats ULA as a special tax because its revenue is earmarked for housing and homelessness programs. A footnote defines a special tax as one "imposed for a specific purpose." Section 4 bars local governments from these taxes, but not voters.

*I'm not a lawyer, so this summarizes the page's text rather than offering legal advice. The page doesn't show subsequent history, so check the decision's current status before relying on it.*

I'm not going to pick yes or no for you on this one. It turns on a values question: whether a simple majority should be enough to approve a special tax for a specific local purpose. Informed Californians disagree on that, and the research doesn't settle it. The facts are clear enough to decide quickly, though.

**Today is Election Day.** Polls close at 8 p.m. local time. The sources I checked conflict on mail-ballot postmark rules, so if you haven't mailed yours, drop it at a county drop box or vote in person before 8 p.m. Your county elections office can confirm.

## The decision rule

- **Yes** if you think a special tax (one earmarked for a specific purpose) should need two-thirds approval no matter who puts it on the ballot. Cities, counties, and special districts already need two-thirds for their own special taxes. Prop 43 makes citizen-led ones match.
- **No** if you think a simple majority of voters should be enough to approve a special tax for a specific local purpose, even if a third of voters oppose it.

## What's settled either way

- It starts January 1, 2027, and covers new, increased, or extended special taxes that voters propose. Renewals are included.
- It isn't retroactive. It doesn't affect existing taxes or measures already on this ballot.
- It doesn't change the majority rule for general taxes, doesn't cut any tax, and doesn't cap transfer-tax rates. A citizen-initiated earmarked transfer tax like LA's ULA would need two-thirds, though.
- The Legislature passed it 35-1 in the Senate and 68-2 in the Assembly, as part of a June deal with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA). HJTA dropped a broader initiative that also targeted transfer taxes and would have applied retroactively.
- Its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, now opposes it, calling it "bad policy" even though she wrote the narrower version.
- The Legislative Analyst says local revenue "could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be," but calls the amount unknown. No official dollar estimate exists.
- Measures that passed by majority but would have failed at two-thirds include LA's "mansion tax" (ULA, about 58% in 2022) and Sonoma County's 2024 wildfire sales tax (62%).

## The strongest case for each side

- **Yes:** Consistency. Two-thirds applies when government places a special tax on the ballot, but appellate courts have held it doesn't apply to voter-placed ones. A 2025 appellate ruling upheld ULA on a majority vote. Supporters argue that narrow majorities in low-turnout elections shouldn't set earmarked taxes for everyone.
- **No:** Majority rule and local services. SPUR says the measure would eliminate "one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues." The official opposing argument says, "Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services." Opponents include firefighters, teachers, SEIU, the state Democratic Party, the counties' association, SPUR, and the author.

## Polling and money

- Berkeley IGS (September): 31% yes, 40% no, 29% undecided.
- PPIC (October, as reported): 42% yes, 55% no among likely voters, down from 43% and 51% in September. Support is 68% among Republicans and 28% among Democrats. I couldn't open PPIC's page to verify this directly.
- Spending: about $15 million for the measure, most of it from the California Business Roundtable's PAC, and about $6 million against.

## What I couldn't verify

- The official argument text and the Tax Policy Center analysis were blocked, so I relied on summaries that quote them.
- Sources describe the 2017 *Upland* ruling differently. CalMatters says the state Supreme Court didn't settle whether citizen-proposed taxes are covered. The Budget Center says it declined review of the lower-court decisions that found they aren't.

Sources:
- [Official voter guide, Prop 43](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/)
- [Official arguments and rebuttals](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)
- [Legislative Analyst's Office, Prop 43 analysis](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026)
- [CalMatters, "Prop. 43 would make special taxes harder to pass"](https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/)

- [LAist, Prop 43 guide](https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-proposition-43-local-special-tax)
- [Court of Appeal, *HJTA v. City of Los Angeles* (2025)](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/ca-court-of-appeal/118063638.html)
- [SPUR voter guide](https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-43-local-tax-threshold)
